readerTitle: The restaurant that isn't failing, and isn't working either
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식당, 가정 청소 업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 망하지 않는 사업이 가장 위험할 수 있다. 이미 자라고 있는 작은 부분이 다음 방향을 알려준다.
misconception: 버티고 있으니 더 열심히 하면 언젠가 좋아진다. 피벗은 처음부터 완전히 새로 시작하는 것이다.

sources.text: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. 피벗 유형 분류 (zoom-in, customer segment 등)

factChecks.note: 월 손익 계산: 매출 $48,000 − 식자재 $15,000 − 인건비 $17,000 − 임대료·공과금 $13,000 = 오너 몫 $3,000. 주 60시간 × 약 4.3주 = 약 260시간, 시간당 약 $11.5. 카드에는 시간당 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
피벗 유형 명칭(zoom-in, customer segment, channel)은 Ries(2011)의 분류를 따랐습니다. 게시 전 ENT-07-02 레슨의 용어와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
좀비 회사의 정의는 ENT-07-03 레슨의 표현(살아남을 만큼은 벌지만 성장하거나 오너에게 보상할 만큼은 못 버는 사업)과 맞췄는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The restaurant that isn't failing, and isn't working either
body: Maya's neighborhood restaurant is three years old. Rent gets paid. Staff get paid. Regulars come on Fridays.
Maya works 60 hours a week and takes home about $3,000 a month. Sales have been flat for 18 months. Nothing is on fire. That may be the problem.

image.label: A tidy, half-empty restaurant on a weeknight
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 작은 동네 식당, 평일 저녁. 테이블 대부분이 비어 있고 한두 테이블만 손님. 주방 쪽에서 오너가 지친 표정으로 장부를 봄. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maya do first?
body: A friend says, "You're surviving. Just push harder: more ads, a new dinner menu."

options.text: Push harder: spend on ads and refresh the dinner menu
options.feedback: Effort feels productive, but 18 flat months suggest more of the same won't change the curve. She'd spend money and energy proving it again.

options.text: Admit it may be a zombie, and look for anything that is growing
options.feedback: This is **zombie companies** at work: a business that survives but doesn't grow. Naming it lets her ask a better question than how to try harder.

options.text: Close now while there's still no debt
options.feedback: Leaving cleanly is a real option, and not having debt helps. But she hasn't yet checked whether any part of the business has a future.

cards.title: A typical month at Maya's.
body: The business covers itself, but barely pays the person running it. Then Maya spots one line that keeps rising: lunch catering for nearby offices went from 2 orders a month to 9 in six months, with no marketing.

cards.title: Why "surviving" is the trap.
body: A **zombie company** earns enough to stay alive but not enough to grow or reward its owner. It rarely forces a decision, so it can drift for years.
The real cost is what Maya isn't doing with her time, savings and energy. A crisis would make her choose. Flat sales let her postpone.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the zombie is the product with flat revenue, steady but low churn, and a founder who keeps shipping small features. Users stay, nobody new arrives, and nothing forces a choice.

cards.title: Which pivot fits what Maya found?
body: Catering is growing on its own. Dinner is flat. Maya wants to change direction without betting everything.

options.text: Turn the kitchen into a full catering business and close dinner next month
options.feedback: Right direction, too fast. Nine orders a month is a signal, not proof, and closing dinner removes her safety net before the test is done.

options.text: Make office lunches the core: a catering menu, a weekday delivery run, dinner only on weekends, tested for 8 weeks
options.feedback: This is a **zoom-in and customer-segment pivot**: one small part becomes the main business, for a new kind of customer. Same kitchen, same skills, a clear test window.

options.text: Switch cuisines to stand out from nearby restaurants
options.feedback: A big change with no evidence behind it. It ignores the one thing customers are already asking for.

cards.title: Set the number before you start.
body: Maya writes down a target before the 8 weeks begin: 25 catering orders a month and at least two offices ordering every week.
If she hits it, she moves more of the business toward catering. If she doesn't, she has learned something real, and closing well becomes an honest option rather than a defeat.

image.label: A calendar with an 8-week test and a target line
image.brief: 8주짜리 달력 인포그래픽. 주마다 작은 도시락 상자 아이콘이 쌓이고, 오른쪽에 "Target: 25 orders / month" 점선. 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: A pivot still has a price.
body: Weekend-only dinners may lose some regulars, and some staff may not want early catering shifts. Office demand can also drop in holiday months, so 8 weeks in December would mislead her.
A pivot keeps what works, but it is not free. Count what you give up, not just what you hope to gain.

cards.title: Now it's a house-cleaning company.
body: Daniel runs a cleaning business with five staff. Revenue has been flat for two years, and he pays himself less than his best cleaner. One thing keeps growing: move-out cleans booked by property managers.

options.text: Offer a property-manager package and test it with three firms for two months
options.feedback: He spots the **zombie** pattern and tries a **customer-segment pivot** toward the part already growing, with a set time and a limit on risk.

options.text: Run a discount to win more household customers
options.feedback: It may add bookings, but at lower prices in the segment that hasn't grown in two years. It feeds the zombie.

options.text: Keep things as they are, since the business pays its bills
options.feedback: Stability has value, and he avoids risk. But he gives up the time he could spend finding out if the growing part could pay him properly.

cards.title: Look for what's growing inside what's stuck.
body: This lesson used two ideas: **zombie companies**, to see that "surviving" is a decision in disguise, and **types of pivots**, to turn one growing part into the next business.
**Try it today:** list your sales by product or customer type for the last six months. Circle anything that grew without much effort.
